added_claim_errors: "The 15-year clock restarts for the new beneficiary" presents an unresolved issue as settled.
"This compresses to four or five years" is unsupported: the key requires at least five; even $8,000 × 4 is only $32,000.
"The money needs to land ... by December 31, 2026" contradicts the April 15, 2027 federal deadline for a designated 2026 rollover, subject to provider processing.
"Scholarships ... don't count" is overbroad: qualifying taxable scholarships and graduate-study stipends can count. Checked [IRS Publication 590-A](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p590a).
"Most [plans] do by 2026, but not all" adds an unverified claim about plan availability.
"The most commonly missed cost" adds an unsupported claim about how frequently state tax is overlooked.
"With distribution code 1 in Box 7" implies a required reporting detail; the code is optional under the [IRS Form 1099-Q instructions](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i1099q).

"Subtract that too" after taking the minimum of all limits can understate eligibility: with $3,000 eligible funds, $7,500 compensation and $2,000 other contributions, the maximum is $3,000, not $1,000.
"Satisfied (opened 2004)" prematurely treats the 15-year test as established without beneficiary history; the later caveat only partially repairs this.
"Scholarships ... do not [count]" is overbroad: qualifying taxable scholarships and graduate-study stipends can count. Checked [IRS Publication 590-A](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p590a).
"He is 22" is not established; someone born in 2004 could still be 21 at the request date.
"Must be completed by December 31, 2026" and "it becomes a 2027 rollover" contradict the federal April 15, 2027 designation window, subject to provider processing.
"Form 1099-Q to you as account owner" is wrong for this direct transfer: the son is the reportable recipient. Checked [IRS Form 1099-Q instructions](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i1099q).
The survey's "30 states" count and complete state classification are not independently verified by the packet or official sources checked; they should not establish 2026 treatment.

"Indiana ... recapture state 529 deductions" misidentifies Indiana's benefit: it is a credit. See [Indiana529's official tax information](https://www.indiana529direct.com/home/help-center-taxes.html).

reasons: Both immediately reject the $48,000 rollover and correctly explain the principal annual, compensation and lifetime restrictions. B narrowly wins because it is substantially less repetitive and avoids A's categorical beneficiary-reset rule and unsupported four-year projection, although B adds calculation and reporting errors. Both incorrectly impose a December deadline and omit the excess Roth contribution's recurring 6% excise tax and correction procedure; neither fully states point 5. I recomputed the arithmetic and opened the IRS sources cited above; B's legislative claim is supported by the official [S. 5550 introduced text](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-119s5550is/html/BILLS-119s5550is.htm), so it is not treated as invented.
